html:
The ruins of a large stone-built town in southeastern Mauritania, widely thought to be the capital of the Ghana Empire described by the Andalusian geographer al-Bakri in 1068.

Al-Bakri wrote of two towns six miles apart, one of Muslim merchants with twelve mosques and one of the king, who controlled the gold that came north from the south. Koumbi Saleh grew rich on the trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt and may have held more than ten thousand people in the 11th century. Digs since 1914 found houses, a mosque and cemeteries. As Ghana weakened, trade moved to Walata and later to the Mali Empire.
sum: The ruins of a large stone-built town in southeastern Mauritania, widely thought to be the capital of the Ghana Empire described by the Andalusian geographer al-Bakri in 1068.
